title.en: The Yellow Emperor Dreams of the Kingdom of Hua-hsü (Liezi)
title.zh: 黃帝夢遊華胥國（列子黃帝篇）

region.en: The kingdom of Hua-hsü, tens of thousands of miles away (symbolic pin: Song, Henan, China)
region.zh: 華胥之國（夢中異域；象徵定位：宋，今河南）

texts.period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book II (The Yellow Emperor)

summary.en: The Yellow Emperor, worn out by three months of fasting in heart after abandoning his schemes, dreams of the kingdom of Hua-hsü beyond the reach of ship or vehicle, where the people have no desires, feel neither joy in life nor abhorrence of death, and bestrode the air as though treading on solid earth. Waking on his throne, he knows the Perfect Way is not to be sought through the senses — and for twenty-eight years there was great orderliness in the Empire.
summary.zh: 黃帝晝寢而夢遊於華胥氏之國——其民無嗜慾，不知樂生，不知惡死；乘空如履實，寢虛若處牀。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon; the Hua-hsü dream is the classic Taoist utopia-vision, tagged otherworld-voyage for the dream-journey cluster. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: For three months he abstained from personal intervention in government. Then he fell asleep in the daytime, and dreamed that he made a journey to the kingdom of Hua-hsü, situated I know not how many tens of thousands of miles distant from the Ch'i State. It was beyond the reach of ship or vehicle or any mortal foot. Only the soul could travel so far.

This kingdom was without head or ruler; it simply went on of itself. Its people were without desires or cravings; they simply followed their natural instincts. They felt neither joy in life nor abhorrence of death; thus they came to no untimely ends. They felt neither attachment to self nor indifference to others; thus they were exempt from love and hatred alike. They knew neither aversion from one course nor inclination to another; hence profit and loss existed not among them.

All were equally untouched by the emotions of love and sympathy, of jealousy and fear. Water had no power to drown them, nor fire to burn; cuts and blows caused them neither injury nor pain, scratching or tickling could not make them itch. They bestrode the air as though treading on solid earth; they were cradled in space as though resting in a bed. Clouds and mist obstructed not their vision, thunder-peals could not stun their ears, physical beauty disturbed not their hearts, mountains and valleys hindered not their steps. They moved about like gods.

When the Yellow Emperor awoke from his dream, he summoned his three Ministers and told them what he had seen. ... Now I know that the Perfect Way is not to be sought through the senses. This Way I know and hold within me, yet I cannot impart it to you. For twenty-eight years after this, there was great orderliness in the Empire, nearly equalling that in the kingdom of Hua-hsü.

title.en: Riding Home on the Wings of the Wind: Lieh Tzŭ's Nine Years (Liezi)
title.zh: 列子御風而行，九年之後（列子黃帝篇）

region.en: Nan-kuo, Lieh Tzŭ's home in Chêng (Zhengzhou, Henan, China)

texts.period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book II (The Yellow Emperor)

summary.en: Lieh Tzŭ, having mastered the system of Lao Shang and Po Kao Tzŭ, rides home on the wings of the wind. His nine-year apprenticeship passes from silence about right and wrong, through the Master's smile, to the seat beside him, until his mind was frozen, his body in dissolution, and he was borne this way and that on the wind like dry chaff or leaves falling from a tree — I knew not whether the wind was riding on me or I on the wind.
summary.zh: 列子師老商子，友伯高子，進二子之道，乘風而歸——九年之後：心凝形釋，骨肉都融；不知風乘我邪？我乘風乎？

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon; the wind-riding motif paralleled in Zhuangzi ch. 1 (skipped to avoid duplication with the chinese record). Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: Lieh Tzu had Lao Shang for his teacher, and Po Kao Tzu for his friend. When he had fully mastered the system of these two philosophers, he rode home again on the wings of the wind. At the end of nine years my mind gave free rein to its reflections, my mouth free passage to its speech. Of right and wrong, profit and loss, I had no knowledge, either as touching myself or others. I knew neither that the Master was my instructor, nor that the other man was my friend. Internal and External were blended into Unity. After that, there was no distinction between eye and ear, ear and nose, nose and mouth: all were the same. My mind was frozen, my body in dissolution, my flesh and bones all melted together.

I was wholly unconscious of what my body was resting on, or what was under my feet. I was borne this way and that on the wind, like dry chaff or leaves falling from a tree. In fact, I knew not whether the wind was riding on me or I on the wind.

title.en: Shang Ch'iu K'ai Walks Through Fire for the Pearl (Liezi)
title.zh: 商丘開下地投水赴火（列子黃帝篇）

region.en: Tzŭ Hua's hall in Chin (Taiyuan, Shanxi, China)
region.zh: 晉國范氏之門（今山西太原）

texts.period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book II (The Yellow Emperor)

summary.en: The starving old man Shang Ch'iu K'ai, jeered by a sorcerer's disciples, is tricked into leaping off a cliff — and is wafted down like a bird, not a bone hurt; into the river for the pearl — and comes up holding it; into a great fire — and returns with his garments unsoiled and his body unsinged. Secret I have none, he answers: my mind was simply One, and material objects thus offered no resistance.
summary.zh: 餓夫商丘開，為幻術之徒所弄；一躍而下，身若飛鳥；入水得珠，赴火不燎——吾心一也，外物不能梗。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon; tagged faith-trial for the ordeal sequence (interpretive). Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: So, by way of a jest, they took the old man with them to the top of a cliff, and the word was passed round that whosoever dared to throw himself over would be rewarded with a hundred ounces of silver. There was an eager response, and Shang Ch'iu K'ai, in perfect good faith, was the first to leap over the edge. And lo! he was wafted down to earth like a bird on the wing, not a bone or muscle of his body being hurt. Mr. Fan's disciples, regarding this as a lucky chance, were merely surprised, but not yet moved to great wonder.

Then they pointed to a bend in the foaming river below, saying: "There is a precious pearl at the bottom of that river, which can be had for the diving." Shang Ch'iu K'ai again acted on their suggestion and plunged in. And when he came out, sure enough he held a pearl in his hand. Then, at last, the whole company began to suspect the truth, and Tzu Hua gave orders that an array of costly viands and silken raiment should be prepared; then suddenly a great fire was kindled round the pile. "If you can walk through the midst of these flames," he said, "you are welcome to keep what you can get of these embroidered stuffs." Without moving a muscle of his face, Shang Ch'iu K'ai walked straight into the fire, and came back again with his garments unsoiled and his body unsinged.

"Secret I have none," replied Shang Ch'iu K'ai. "Even in my own mind I have no clue as to the real cause. ... I knew not what part of space my body occupied, nor yet where danger lurked. My mind was simply One, and material objects thus offered no resistance. That is all. But now, having discovered that your disciples were deceiving me, my inner man is thrown into a state of doubt and perplexity, while outwardly my senses of sight and hearing re-assert themselves. When I reflect that I have just had a providential escape from being drowned and burned to death, my heart within me freezes with horror, and my limbs tremble with fear. I shall never again have the courage to go near water or fire."

title.en: The Tiger-Feeder Who Was Neither Antagonistic Nor Compliant (Liezi)
title.zh: 梁鴦養虎：不逆不順（列子黃帝篇）

region.en: King Hsüan's park-enclosure (symbolic pin: Xi'an, Shaanxi, China)
region.zh: 周宣王之囿（象徵定位：陝西西安）

texts.period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book II (The Yellow Emperor)

summary.en: Liang Yang, skilled in the management of wild birds and beasts, feeds tigers and wolves, eagles and ospreys in King Hsüan's park without one clawing or biting another. His method: avoid giving live animals or whole carcasses, time their hunger and repletion, and be neither antagonistic nor compliant, so that the animals regard me as one of themselves.
summary.zh: 周宣王之牧正有役人梁鴦者，能養野禽獸——養虎之法：不逆其怒，不順其喜；虎可與遊者，必順其性也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon; paralleled in Zhuangzi ch. 19 tiger-passage. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: The Keeper of Animals under King Hsüan, of the Chou dynasty, had an assistant named Liang Yang, who was skilled in the management of wild birds and beasts. When he fed them in their park-enclosure, all the animals showed themselves tame and tractable, although they comprised tigers, wolves, eagles and ospreys. Male and female freely propagated their kind, and their numbers multiplied. The different species lived promiscuously together, yet they never clawed nor bit one another.

In feeding tigers, then, I avoid giving them either live animals or whole carcasses, lest in the former case the act of killing, in the latter the act of tearing them to pieces, should excite them to fury. Again, I time their periods of hunger and repletion, and I gain a full understanding of the causes of their anger. Tigers are of a different species from man, but, like him, they are docile with those who treat them kindly, though they will show fight when their lives are attacked.

Hence it is my aim to be neither antagonistic nor compliant, so that the animals regard me as one of themselves. Thus it happens that they walk about the park without regretting the tall forests and the broad marshes, and rest in the enclosure without yearning for the lonely mountains and the dark valleys. Such is the effect of using one's common sense.

title.en: The Sailor and the Sea-Gulls That Would Not Alight (Liezi)
title.zh: 海上之人好鷗鳥者（列子黃帝篇）

region.en: The sea-shore (symbolic pin: Yantai, Shandong, China)
region.zh: 海濱（象徵定位：山東煙臺）

texts.period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book II (The Yellow Emperor)

summary.en: The sailor swam daily in the sea-gulls' midst, a hundred gulls and more flocking about him — until his father asked him to catch one or two for pets. The next day the gulls only wheeled about in the air and would not alight.
summary.zh: 海上之人有好漚鳥者，每旦之海上，從漚鳥遊；漚鳥之至者百住而不止。其父曰：吾聞漚鳥皆從汝遊，汝取來吾玩之。明日之海上，漚鳥舞而不下也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon; the 'birds dance but will not descend' (ou-wu-wu-hsia) became a proverb for self-conscious scheming. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: There was once a man, a sailor by profession, who was very fond of sea-gulls. Every morning he went into the sea and swam about in their midst, at which times a hundred gulls and more would constantly flock about him. One day his father said to him: "I am told that sea-gulls swim about with you in the water. I wish you would catch one or two for me to make pets of." On the following day, the sailor went down to the sea as usual, but lo! the gulls only wheeled about in the air and would not alight.

title.en: The Man Who Came Out of the Rock and Walked Through Fire (Liezi)
title.zh: 趙襄子率徒狩山中，石中生人（列子黃帝篇）

region.en: The Central Mountains of Chao (Hengshan, Shanxi, China)
region.zh: 趙之中山（象徵定位：山西恆山）

texts.period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book II (The Yellow Emperor)

summary.en: Hunting with a hundred thousand men in the Central Mountains, Chao Hsiang Tzŭ's party fire the forest, and a man appears, emerging from a rocky cliff to hover in the air amidst flames and smoke. What do you mean by rock? what do you mean by fire? he asks — I know nothing of them. Tzŭ Hsia tells Marquis Wên that the Master is able to do these things, but he is also able to refrain from doing them.
summary.zh: 趙襄子率徒十萬狩於中山，藉芿燔林——有一人從石壁中出，隨煙火上下，若無所傷。襄子曰：石？火？其人曰：不知也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon; tagged faith-trial for the fire-ordeal. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: Chao Hsiang Tzu led out a company of a hundred thousand men to hunt in the Central Mountains. They dropped sparks in the undergrowth, which set fire to the whole forest, and the glow of the flames was visible for a hundred miles around. Suddenly a man appeared, emerging from a rocky cliff, and was seen to hover in the air amidst the flames and the smoke. Everybody took him for a disembodied spirit. When the fire had passed, he walked quietly out, and showed no trace of having been through the ordeal.

So the prince inquired what secret power it was that enabled him to dwell in rock and to walk through fire. "What do you mean by rock?" replied the man; "what do you mean by fire?" "What you just now came out of is rock; what you just now walked through fire." "I know nothing of them," replied the man.

"From what I have heard the Master say," replied Tzu Hsia, "the man who achieves harmony with Tao enters into close unison with external objects, and none of them has the power to harm or hinder him. Passing through solid metal or stone, walking in the midst of fire or on the surface of water— all these things become possible to him." ... "The Master," replied Tzu Hsia, "is able to do these things, but he is also able to refrain from doing them." Which answer hugely delighted the Marquis.

title.en: P'ao Hsi, Nü Kua, and Shên Nung with Serpents' Bodies (Liezi)
title.zh: 庖犧氏女媧氏神農氏，蛇身人面（列子黃帝篇）

region.en: The demi-gods of remote antiquity (symbolic pin: Tianshui, Gansu, China)
region.zh: 上古神人（象徵定位：甘肅天水）

texts.period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book II (The Yellow Emperor)

summary.en: Outward form is no criterion: P'ao Hsi, Nü Kua, Shên Nung and Hsia Hou had serpents' bodies, human faces, ox-heads and tigers' snouts — their forms were not human, yet their virtue was of the saintliest; while Chieh and Chou, in all external respects like other men, had the minds of savage brutes.
summary.zh: 庖犧氏、女媧氏、神農氏、夏后氏，蛇身人面，牛首虎鼻——此有非人之狀，而有大聖之德。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon; the demi-god catalogue cross-linked to the chinese tradition's Nüwa records. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: P'ao Hsi, Nil Kua, Shen Nung and Hsia Hou had serpents' bodies, human faces, ox-heads and tigers' snouts. Thus, their forms were not human, yet their virtue was of the saintliest. Chieh of the Hsia dynasty, Chou of the Yin, Huan of the Lu State, and Mu of the Ch'u State, were in all external respects, as facial appearance and possession of the seven channels of sense, like unto other men; yet they had the minds of savage brutes.

title.en: The Yellow Emperor's Beast-Army and K'uei's Musical Stone (Liezi)
title.zh: 黃帝熊羆貔貅貙虎前驅，夔擊石拊石（列子黃帝篇）

region.en: The field of P'an-ch'üan (Banquan, Hebei/Shanxi, China)
region.zh: 阪泉之野（今河北／山西阪泉）

texts.period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book II (The Yellow Emperor)

summary.en: When the Yellow Emperor fought with Yen Ti on the field of P'an-ch'üan, his vanguard was composed of bears, wolves, panthers, lynxes and tigers, his ensign-bearers eagles, ospreys, falcons and kites. And when K'uei tapped the musical stone in varying cadence, all the animals danced to the sound; the strains of the Shao on the flute brought the phœnix itself flying down to assist.
summary.zh: 黃帝與炎帝戰於阪泉之野，帥熊羆狼豹貙虎為前驅——堯使夔典樂，擊石拊石，百獸率舞；簫韶九成，鳳凰來儀。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon; the beast-army of the Yanhuang war, retold from Liezi. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: When the Yellow Emperor fought with Yen Ti on the field of P'an-ch'iian, his vanguard was composed of bears, wolves, panthers, lynxes and tigers, while his ensign-bearers were eagles, ospreys, falcons and kites. This was forcible impressment of animals into the service of man. The Emperor Yao entrusted K'uei with the regulation of music.

When the latter tapped the musical stone in varying cadence, all the animals danced to the sound of the music. When the strains of the Shao were heard on the flute, the phœnix itself flew down to assist. This was the attraction of animals by the power of music. In what, then, do the minds of birds and beasts differ from the minds of men?
